title: Napkin Math

post.author: u/cab_radio_bronagh
post.title: I dispatch nights for a cab firm. I sized our New Year's Eve phone lines on a napkin. At 2 AM every line was busy, and the booking robot rang me with my own voice.

blocks.text: I run the night desk at Coldharbour Cars: a radio, two screens and a kettle above a launderette on Coldharbour Road. In the autumn we swapped the old switchboard for a phone company's booking robot. It answers each call, records your pickup address in the five seconds after the tone, and books the cab. We rent lines from the phone company, and each line holds one call at a time. When every line is busy, the robot offers a ring-back instead: it keeps your recording, rings you back in turn, and plays your own words to you to confirm.

In December Mr Vasko, who owns the firm, asked how many lines to rent for New Year's Eve. Last year's bill said 14,400 calls, all between 8 PM and 4 AM. I worked it out on a napkin from the chip shop:

blocks.title: NEW YEAR'S EVE: HOW MANY LINES
items: A CALL HOLDS A LINE 2 MINUTES, SO A LINE TAKES 30 AN HOUR

blocks.text: Until one o'clock the night ran smoothly. Then the fireworks crowds came out of the park. This is the phone company's dashboard for the night:

20:00-04:00  calls offered        14,400
01:00-02:00  calls offered         5,400
01:00-02:00  got a line            1,800
01:00-02:00  sent to ring-back     3,600
02:00:00     lines busy         60 of 60
02:00:00     ring-backs waiting    3,600

At one I had rung our own number from my mobile, to hear what callers hear. Every line was busy, so I said the office's address after the tone and hung up. At two my mobile rang. It was the robot, playing me my own voice, an hour old, asking for a cab to come and fetch me from the desk I was sitting at.
It sounded like someone who had been waiting a long time.

At four, when I lifted the radio to switch it off, there was another napkin under it, brown at the edges, in the capitals of Ignatius, who ran this desk from 1971 to 2009. It was dated 31 December 1999 and said only: *Not the night. The hour after one.*
Mr Vasko wants next year's number by Friday. How many lines should we rent, and where did my napkin go wrong?

blocks.label: phone_dashboard_0200.png

diagram.aria: The phone company's dashboard for New Year's Eve, 01:00 to 02:00. Callers make 5,400 calls in the hour, 1.5 a second. The booking robot has 60 lines, each carrying 30 calls an hour, and all 60 are busy at 02:00. 1,800 calls got a line and booked a cab. 3,600 found every line full and were sent to the ring-back queue, where 3,600 recordings are waiting at 02:00.

blocks.caption: The phone company's dashboard, redrawn. In the hour after one, 5,400 calls arrived, 1.5 a second. Sixty lines, each holding a call for 2 minutes, carry 30 calls an hour each, 1,800 in all. The other 3,600 callers found every line full and went into the ring-back queue, and at 2:00 all 60 lines were busy and 3,600 recordings were waiting their turn.

comments.author: u/grey_pager
comments.text: A sum on a napkin is what engineers call a back-of-the-envelope estimate, and yours has the right shape: how many calls arrive, divided by how many one line can carry. Two more words. Your 0.5 a second is an average: the night's calls spread evenly over all eight hours. A peak is the busiest stretch, here an hour, and the peak factor is how many times the average that stretch runs. Now read your dashboard. 5,400 calls in the hour after one: how many a second is that, and how many times your 0.5? How many lines would that hour keep busy? And at exactly 0.5 a second, the average you planned for, how busy were your 60 lines?

replies.author: u/cab_radio_bronagh
replies.text: I did the first two on the back of the same napkin. Then the last one, and I had to sit down. Mr Vasko asked me who Ignatius was. He bought the firm in 2012, and he says nobody of that name is in any of the old rotas.

comments.author: u/trunk_line_gethin
comments.text: Phone engineer here, now sizing systems for a company that carries calls over the internet. When you redo the napkin, carry the units through every line, because that's where napkins usually go wrong. Our robots record at 64 kilobits a second. Bits, not bytes: a byte is 8 bits, so that's 8 kilobytes a second, and a five-second address is 40 KB, not 320. Line speeds are sold in bits and disks in bytes, so mixing them is out by 8 every time. A KB is 1,000 bytes and a KiB, a kibibyte, is 1,024, about 2.4% apart, and the gap grows at every step to about 10% by terabytes, trillions of bytes. For storage, multiply each recording's size by how many you write, by the retention, how long you must keep them, and by the copies the provider keeps. And if you ever add an app, count its read:write ratio: how many requests only look something up, the reads, for every one that saves something, a write. What does your contract say about recordings?

replies.author: u/cab_radio_bronagh
replies.text: 64 kilobits a second, kept for a year, in two copies. The ring-back queue kept mine for an hour.

comments.author: u/peak_hour_imelda
comments.text: I plan the phone lines for a council's out-of-hours line, where the busiest night of the year is the first hard frost. Two habits. Never guess the peak when you have records: your bill has the calls hour by hour, so find the busiest hour and divide it by the night's average, and that's your peak factor. Then look inside that hour, because its busiest minutes run hotter than its average. And write the napkin into the plan, every assumption on its own line with its unit, and a date to check it against the next bill. A wrong number should be caught in January by whoever reads the plan, not at two in the morning by a robot.

comments.author: u/spare_cab_zdenka
comments.text: I run eleven cabs out of a garage in the next town. I gave up on sums years ago. The phone company sells lines by the night, so I rent the most it will sell me for the whole holiday week and sleep. Nobody has been sent to ring-back on my watch.

reply.prompt: Mr Vasko wants next year's number by Friday. What should Bronagh tell him? Part 2 follows your advice.

options.text: Size it for the hour after one: 5,400 calls at 30 an hour per line is 180 lines busy. Rent 225 for that night, so they're at most 80% busy.
options.part2: Mr Vasko rented 225 lines for New Year's Eve and kept 60 for every other night. 14,400 calls came between eight and four again, 5,400 of them in the hour after one, 1.5 a second. At the busiest moment 180 of the 225 lines were busy, 45 were free for the minutes that ran hotter, and the ring-back counter stayed at 0 all night. This time the napkin went into the plan, every line of it: last year's bill, the hour after one, 30 calls an hour per line, at most 80% busy, and a date in January to check it against the new bill. At two my mobile rang. Nobody spoke, just the hiss the old radio used to make between calls. Then a man's slow voice said, *Base, all clear,* and the line went dead. I've pinned both napkins above the radio.
options.senior: The napkin's method was sound and its question was wrong: lines have to fit the busiest hour, not the night's average. 5,400 calls an hour at 30 per line is 180 busy, the same as 1.5 calls a second times 120 seconds each. Headroom covers what the hour's average hides: its busiest minutes, a bigger year, a line that fails. Renting for the one night keeps the cost to the night that needs it, and writing the napkin down lets someone check every assumption before the next one.

options.text: Keep the napkin, since its sums were right, and double it for a busier year: rent 120 lines. A margin that size covers any night's surprises.
options.part2: Mr Vasko rented 120 lines. 14,400 calls came again, and until one there was room to spare. From one, 1.5 calls a second arrived and 120 lines carried 1 a second, 3,600 an hour: in the hour after one, 1,800 callers were sent to ring-back, and at two every line was busy again. The ring-backs began at two, oldest first. At ten past, my mobile rang. I hadn't rung our line this year. The robot played me my own voice anyway, saying the office's address, exactly as I'd said it last New Year's Eve.
options.senior: Doubling a wrong number gives a bigger wrong number. The napkin sized the lines for the night's average hour, and the hour after one runs at three times that, so twice the average still left a third of that hour's callers waiting. A margin covers surprises around the right estimate; it can't fix an estimate of the wrong thing. Find the busiest hour first, then put the margin on top of it.

options.text: Size it for the hour after one: 5,400 calls at 30 an hour per line is 180 lines busy. Rent exactly 180 for that night, so not one sits idle.
options.verdict: Trade-off: the right load, no room
options.part2: Mr Vasko rented 180 lines for the night. 14,400 calls came again, 5,400 in the hour after one, and 180 lines carry exactly 5,400 an hour, so on the hour's average they fitted to the call: 180 of 180 busy. But calls don't arrive on an average. They came in clumps: when the fireworks ended, when the pubs called time, when the last bus didn't come. In every clump the next callers found all 180 lines full and heard the ring-back offer, and the dashboard's ring-back counter ticked up in bursts all through the hour. At two my mobile rang. The robot played a voice that wasn't mine, giving our address slowly, the way Ignatius wrote.
options.senior: 180 is the right estimate of the busiest hour's load and the wrong number to rent. Lines that are 100% busy on the hour's average are full in every minute that runs above it, and calls never arrive evenly. Headroom, at most 80% busy here, a teaching model's number rather than a law, is what absorbs the clumps, a bigger year and a line that fails. Estimate the peak, then leave room on top of it.

options.text: Skip the napkin: rent the most lines the phone company sells, 500, for the whole holiday week, so nobody is ever sent to ring-back again.
options.part2: Mr Vasko rented 500 lines for the holiday week. Nobody was sent to ring-back all week. In the hour after one, 5,400 calls came, and at the busiest moment 180 lines were busy and 320 sat silent. On the other six nights most of the 500 never rang once. The bill was the biggest the firm has ever had from the phone company, and in January Mr Vasko asked how many lines we had actually needed. I couldn't tell him, because nobody had done the sum. At two on New Year's Eve, every one of the 320 silent lines showed busy for a single second, all together, then went quiet again.
options.senior: Buying far more than you need is a fair answer when it's cheap, short and you know the margin. Here it bought certainty without knowledge: 500 lines was about 2.8 times the 180 the busiest hour needed, and nobody knew whether that was plenty or not enough for a bigger year, so next year's bill or next year's crowd decides for you. Do the napkin first, then choose your margin on purpose.

sim.title: The estimation workbench
sim.lede: You're Bronagh with a clean napkin. This workbench does the sums on the case's numbers, or on yours. Start from Coldharbour Cars on New Year's Eve: each call is one user making one request, every call is a write because the robot saves a 40 KB recording of the address, a line carries one call per 120 seconds (30 an hour), and the calls come in 8 hours with a peak factor of 3. Or start from a link shortener at 100 million requests a day, like Loadout's Build Night L3: 10 million users making 10 requests each, 100 reads for every write, 500 bytes a link, kept 5 years in 3 copies, a peak factor of 2 and 1,000 requests a second per server, all teaching-model values. The sums: requests a day are users times requests each. The average a second divides them by the seconds in the hours the traffic comes in, and 24 hours is 86,400 seconds. The peak multiplies the average by the peak factor. Servers busy at the peak divide it by what one server carries, and servers to run keep them at most 80% busy, the room to spare from the ticket booth's case. Storage is the size of each write times the writes, times 365 for a year, times the retention and the copies, and assumes every day looks like the one described. Bandwidth at the peak is reads a second times the size going out, and writes a second times the size coming in, times 8 for bits. KB, MB, GB and TB count in 1,000s. Every figure is rounded to three figures, so 1,157.4 shows as 1,160, and the napkin also gives the exact one. Your plan checks a number of servers, or lines, against the true peak. The capacities are teaching-model values, and the mistakes menu makes one error on purpose and shows how far off it lands.
sim.tryThis: Try this: on Coldharbour's night, read the napkin top to bottom: 0.5 a second, 1.5 at the peak, 5,400 in the hour after one, 180 lines busy and 225 to run. Your plan starts at the 60 lines Bronagh rented: 3,600 sent to ring-back. Pick the dispatcher's napkin from the mistakes: 60 lines, 3 times short. Set the plan to 120, 180, 225 and 500 and read what each does at the peak. Try a whole day's 86,400 seconds, then dividing by 3,600 alone. Then switch to the link shortener: 1,157.4 a second, about 1,160, 2.71 TB of storage and 9.17 Mbps out at the peak. Pick bits for bytes, KiB for KB and forgotten copies, and read how far off each lands. Last, move any input and watch every line of the napkin follow.

explain.oneLine: Nothing on the line was haunted. Bronagh's napkin sized the lines for the night's average, 0.5 calls a second, and the hour after one brought 1.5: three times what 60 lines could carry. Every extra caller joined the ring-back queue, and a queue hands back what went in, late.

steps.title: Per day to per second: divide, and round on purpose.
steps.text: Traffic is usually counted per day and servers are sized per second, so the first move is a division. A day has 86,400 seconds: 100 million requests a day is 100,000,000 ÷ 86,400 = 1,157.4 a second, about 1,160. Round on purpose to check it. 100 million is 1 followed by 8 zeros, and a day is about 100,000 seconds, 1 followed by 5, so the answer is about 1 followed by 3: a thousand. If your exact answer isn't near that, a step is wrong. But divide by the seconds the traffic really comes in. Coldharbour's 14,400 calls all came between 8 PM and 4 AM, 28,800 seconds: 0.5 a second. A whole day's 86,400 would give 0.167, one every 6 seconds, a third of the truth. Dividing by 3,600 alone treats the eight hours as one and gives 4 a second, eight times too many. Bronagh got this step right.

steps.title: Size for the peak, then leave room.
steps.text: An average spreads the traffic evenly, and nothing real arrives that way. The peak factor says how many times the average the busiest stretch runs, and if you have records you read it from them. Coldharbour's hour after one carried 5,400 calls, 1.5 a second, three times the night's average. What you need is the peak divided by what one server carries. A line holds each call 120 seconds, so it carries 30 an hour, and 5,400 ÷ 30 = 180 lines busy at the peak. The same 180 comes from 1.5 calls a second × 120 seconds on a line, which is Little's law: the number in a system is the rate things arrive times how long each stays. Then leave headroom: at most 80% busy, the room to spare from the ticket booth's case, is 180 ÷ 0.8 = 225 lines. Bronagh's 60 was a third of the peak, and 100% busy even on an average hour. The ring-back queue is why she heard herself an hour late. In the hour after one, 1 call a second more arrived than 60 lines carry, so 3,600 recordings piled up, and no line came free for a ring-back until the rush ended at two. Then the robot started at the front, with the people who had called at one, Bronagh among them. A queue adds waiting, not capacity: what comes out is what went in, late.

steps.title: Then reads and writes, storage and bandwidth.
steps.text: The read:write ratio splits requests by what they do. A link shortener with 100 reads for every write gets, of 100 million requests a day, 990,099 writes, links created, and about 99 million reads, links followed: you size the reads for speed and the writes for storage. Storage follows the writes: size × writes a day × 365 for a year, then × the years of retention × the copies. At 500 bytes a link, a teaching value for the long address, the short code and a date, that's 495 MB a day, 181 GB a year, and 2.71 TB for 5 years in 3 copies. Bandwidth follows the peak: requests a second × size. With a peak factor of 2, another teaching value, about 2,290 reads a second × 500 bytes is 1.15 MB a second out, 9.17 Mbps once you multiply by 8 for bits. Coldharbour's recordings are the same sum: 14,400 a night × 40 KB is 576 MB, kept a year in two copies.

steps.title: The units traps.
steps.text: Most napkins that go wrong go wrong in their units. Per day against per second is a factor of 86,400, and a night against a day is 24 ÷ the night's hours: 3 for Coldharbour's 8. Bits against bytes is 8: links are sold in bits a second and disks in bytes, and 64 kilobits a second is 8 kilobytes. KB against KiB, 1,000 bytes against 1,024, is 2.4% at kilobytes and nearly 10% at terabytes, so 1 TB is about 0.91 TiB (931 GiB). Then the two everyone forgets: copies, which multiply storage by 2 or 3, and peaks, which multiply rates by whatever the busiest hour says. Write the unit next to every number. A mistake then shows up as a unit that doesn't cancel, like calls a day divided by the seconds in an hour.

steps.title: Know the numbers, and estimate before you build.
steps.text: Latency has its own napkin. Jeff Dean's 2009 slide, which the warehouse case in Season 1 met, lists a main memory reference at 100 ns, reading 1 MB sequentially from memory at 250,000 ns, a round trip within the same datacenter at 500,000 ns, a disk seek at 10,000,000 ns, and a packet from California to the Netherlands and back at 150,000,000 ns. The copy most engineers share, a GitHub gist labelled ~2012, adds SSD rows: reading 4K randomly from an SSD at 150,000 ns, and 1 MB sequentially at 1,000,000 ns, for an SSD of about 1 GB a second. They're approximate and dated, and hardware has moved since, but the gaps between them still choose designs: in that list, reading 1 MB from disk takes 80 times as long as from memory, and 20 times as long as from an SSD. That's the point of estimating before you build. A page of arithmetic picks the design's shape, one server or many, a cache or not, whether the data fits on one machine, while changing your mind is still cheap. Then measure, with a load test and the real dashboards, and correct the napkin. You'll build both halves in Loadout: Build Night L1 is the simulation core, and L3 runs a URL shortener at 100 million requests a day.

diagram.aria: The fix, drawn for the hour after one next New Year's Eve. Callers make 5,400 calls in the hour, 1.5 a second. The booking robot has 225 lines, each carrying 30 calls an hour, and at most 180 are busy, 80%. All 5,400 calls get a line and book a cab. The ring-back queue stays empty, with 45 lines to spare.

explain.caption: The fix, drawn for the hour after one next New Year's Eve. 5,400 calls arrive, 1.5 a second. 225 lines carry 30 calls an hour each, 6,750 an hour, so at the busiest moment 180 are busy, 80%, and 45 are spare for the minutes that run hotter than the hour. Nobody is sent to ring-back.

fix.title: The fix: size the lines for the busiest hour, leave headroom, and write the napkin into the plan
fix.text: Take the peak from the records: the bill shows the hour after one at 5,400 calls, 1.5 a second. Divide by what one line carries, 30 calls an hour, for 180 lines busy, and leave headroom so they're at most 80% busy: 225 lines. Rent them for New Year's Eve only, since the phone company sells lines by the night, and keep 60 for ordinary nights. Write the napkin into the plan with every assumption and its unit, the source of each number, and a date to check it against the next bill, so a wrong number is caught in January by a reader, not at 2 AM by a robot. If the ring-back queue stays, tell each caller their place and their wait, so a ring-back an hour later is a promise kept, not a ghost.

limits: An estimate is only as good as its inputs. Last year's 14,400 calls say nothing about a fireworks display moving to a bigger park. Google's SRE book counts inorganic demand, events like launches and campaigns, as its own step in capacity planning. Check the napkin against the records every year.

The busiest hour's average still hides its busiest minutes, and calls never arrive evenly. That is what the 80% is for, and 80% is a teaching value, not a law. To size something that must not fail, measure it with a load test or work it out with proper queuing tables.

Requests per second treats every request as the same size. Google's SRE book warns that modeling capacity as queries per second often makes for a poor metric, because requests cost different amounts and the mix changes; it measures capacity in resources such as CPU cores and memory.

explain.seniorTake: Estimation is a habit, not a trick. Before you build or buy, write the napkin: state every assumption (users, requests each, the hours they arrive in, the peak factor, the size of each write, retention, copies, what one server carries), round to powers of ten on purpose, and carry the units through every line so a slip shows. Size rates for the busiest hour, not the day, and put headroom on top. Then sanity-check against something you know, such as last year's bill, a dashboard or a latency number, and let the result pick the design's shape: one box or many, a cache or not. Keep the napkin in the design doc with a date, so the first load test or the next bill can prove it wrong while that's still cheap.

realWorld.title: Jeff Dean: estimate before you build
realWorld.text: In his keynote at LADIS 2009, Designs, Lessons and Advice from Building Large Distributed Systems, Jeff Dean, then a Google Fellow, has a slide called Designing Efficient Systems. It asks how, given a basic problem definition, you choose the best solution, and names an "Important skill: ability to estimate performance of a system design", "without actually having to build it!" The next slide, Numbers Everyone Should Know, lists among others: main memory reference 100 ns; read 1 MB sequentially from memory 250,000 ns; round trip within same datacenter 500,000 ns; disk seek 10,000,000 ns; read 1 MB sequentially from disk 20,000,000 ns; and send packet CA to Netherlands to CA 150,000,000 ns. They are rough numbers from 2009, not a measurement of today's hardware.

realWorld.title: Dean's thumbnails: two designs, two lines of arithmetic
realWorld.text: A later slide, Back of the Envelope Calculations, asks how long it takes to generate an image results page of 30 thumbnails. Design 1 reads serially and thumbnails 256K images on the fly: 30 seeks × 10 ms/seek + 30 × 256K / 30 MB/s = 560 ms. Design 2 issues the reads in parallel: 10 ms/seek + 256K read / 30 MB/s = 18 ms, with the note that it ignores variance, so really more like 30-60 ms, probably. The slide lists variations, such as caching single images or whole sets of thumbnails and pre-computing thumbnails, and its last line begins: back of the envelope helps identify most promising. The first sum is 300 ms of seeks plus about 256 ms of reading, written as 560: rounded on purpose.

realWorld.title: Know your building blocks
realWorld.text: Dean's slide Know Your Basic Building Blocks lists Google's core libraries and storage systems and asks you to understand not just their interfaces but their implementations, at least at a high level, because, in its words, if you don't know what's going on, you can't do decent back-of-the-envelope calculations. The capacity per server in this case's sim is a teaching value for exactly that reason: the real number comes from knowing, or measuring, what your server does with each request.

realWorld.title: Google's SRE book on demand forecasting
realWorld.text: Chapter 1 of Google's Site Reliability Engineering book, written by Benjamin Treynor Sloss, says: "Demand forecasting and capacity planning can be viewed as ensuring that there is sufficient capacity and redundancy to serve projected future demand with the required availability." It adds that a surprising number of services and teams don't take the steps necessary to ensure that the required capacity is in place by the time it is needed. It counts both organic growth, from natural product adoption and usage, and inorganic growth, from events like feature launches and marketing campaigns, and lists mandatory steps: an accurate organic demand forecast that extends beyond the lead time required for acquiring capacity, an accurate incorporation of inorganic demand sources, and regular load testing of the system to correlate raw capacity (servers, disks, and so on) to service capacity.

realWorld.title: A napkin inside Google's load balancing
realWorld.text: In the SRE book's Handling Overload chapter, Alejandro Forero Cuervo gives a one-line napkin: if a datacenter runs 100 backend tasks and each task can process up to 500 requests per second, the load balancing algorithm will not allow more than 50,000 queries per second to be sent to that datacenter. The same chapter warns, under The Pitfalls of Queries per Second, that different queries can have vastly different resource requirements, and that Google learned the hard way that modeling capacity as queries per second often makes for a poor metric. Its better solution is to measure capacity directly in available resources, such as CPU cores and memory.

realWorld.title: Little's law
realWorld.text: In 1961 John D. C. Little published a proof of the queuing formula L = λW. In a paper for its fiftieth anniversary he writes that it has become widely known as Little's Law, that it is basically a theorem in queuing theory, and that it became well known because of its theoretical and practical importance. L is the average number in a system, λ (lambda) the rate things arrive, and W the average time each spends inside. Coldharbour's 1.5 calls a second × 120 seconds on a line is 180 calls on lines at once, the same 180 the hourly napkin gives.

realWorld.title: The shared copy, with SSDs
realWorld.text: The version of the list most engineers pass around is a GitHub gist by Jonas Bonér, Latency Numbers Every Programmer Should Know. Its table is headed Latency Comparison Numbers (~2012) and credits Jeff Dean, and Peter Norvig as the original author. Besides Dean's rows it lists read 4K randomly from SSD at 150,000 ns and read 1 MB sequentially from SSD at 1,000,000 ns, both annotated ~1GB/sec SSD, and notes beside the disk row that reading 1 MB sequentially from disk is 80x memory, 20X SSD. The table keeps growing: as it reads today it also has rows for language models marked 2026. Treat every row as a dated order of magnitude.

asked: Estimate the requests per second and the storage for a URL shortener that creates 100 million new links a month.
How many servers would it need, and would you put a cache in front?
How do you know your estimate is right?
interview.answer: Say the method out loud, then the numbers. Assumptions first, each one a guess to check later: 100 million new links a month, 100 reads for every write, 500 bytes a link, kept 5 years in 3 copies, a peak of twice the average, and 1,000 requests a second per server. A month is about 30 × 86,400, roughly 2.6 million seconds, so writes are 100 million ÷ 2.6 million, about 40 a second, and reads are 100 times that, about 4,000 a second, 8,000 at the peak. Storage: 100 million × 500 bytes is 50 GB a month, 600 GB a year, 3 TB over 5 years, 9 TB with 3 copies. Bandwidth out at the peak: 8,000 × 500 bytes is 4 MB a second, 32 Mbps. Servers: 8,000 ÷ 1,000 is 8 busy, 10 to stay at most 80% busy. Then sanity-check. One machine's disk could hold years of links, so storage isn't the hard part; the reads are, and links rarely change, so a cache in front, as in the bakery's case, takes most of them. Say which number you're least sure of, usually the peak factor, and how you'd check it: a load test before launch, the real dashboards after. You'll build exactly this in Loadout: Build Night L1 is the simulation core, and L3 runs a URL shortener at 100 million requests a day.

The old equipment that connected incoming phone calls to the desk's phones.
Coldharbour's automated phone service: it answers each call, records the pickup address in the five seconds after the tone, and books the cab.
One call's worth of capacity rented from a phone company. Each line holds one call at a time, so 60 lines hold 60 calls at once.
The robot's queue for callers who find every line busy: it keeps their recording, rings them back in turn, and plays their own words to confirm.
A list of who works which shifts.
A quick estimate with round numbers and stated assumptions, done before building, to find a design's size and shape. Also called napkin math.
Another name for a back-of-the-envelope estimate.
A total spread evenly over a stretch of time: 14,400 calls over 8 hours is 1,800 an hour, 0.5 a second.
How many times the average the busiest stretch runs. At Coldharbour the hour after one ran at 3 times the night's average.
The hour with the most traffic, usually the peak you size servers or lines for.
A number such as 10, 1,000 or 100,000: 1 followed by zeros. Rounding to powers of ten makes an estimate quick to check.
A quick test of whether an answer is plausible, against something you already know, such as last year's bill or a power-of-ten guess.
A read is a request that only looks something up, such as following a short link. A write saves or changes something, such as creating one.
How many reads arrive for every write. A link shortener might see 100 reads for each write; Coldharbour's robot writes on every call, so it has 0 reads for each.
How long data must be kept before it may be deleted, such as a year for Coldharbour's call recordings.
How many copies of each piece of data a store keeps, on different disks or machines, so one failure loses nothing. Storage multiplies by the number of copies.
A thousand bits. 64 kilobits a second is 8 kilobytes a second, because a byte is 8 bits.
Kilobits per second: a thousand bits each second. bps is bits per second.
Kibibyte: 1,024 bytes, where a KB is 1,000. MiB, GiB and TiB grow further from MB, GB and TB at every step, nearly 10% apart by terabytes.
A terabyte (TB) is a trillion bytes, or 1,000 GB.
Tebibyte: 1,024 GiB, or 1,099,511,627,776 bytes, about 10% more than a TB. So 1 TB is about 0.91 TiB.
A made-up but plausible number used to show the method, like 1,000 requests a second per server. State it out loud and check it later.
The average number of things in a system equals the rate they arrive times how long each stays: 1.5 calls a second × 120 seconds is 180 calls on lines at once.
The mathematics of waiting lines: how arrival rates, service times and capacity set waits and queue lengths.
A written plan for a system, reviewed before it's built, with its assumptions and estimates on the page so others can check them.
A meeting where a team checks whether its systems can carry the traffic coming, and how the numbers were worked out.
An estimate of how much use is coming, made early enough to have the capacity ready when it arrives.
Making sure there is enough capacity, with room to spare, for the demand you forecast, by the time it arrives.
Google SRE's terms: organic growth comes from natural product adoption and usage; inorganic growth from events like feature launches and marketing campaigns.
How long it takes to get new capacity after you decide you need it, such as ordering and installing servers.
In Google's SRE book, raw capacity is servers, disks and so on; service capacity is how much real traffic they can serve. Load testing links the two.
Spare copies of a part, so the system keeps working when one fails.
The share of time a system works when people need it.
In Google's SRE book, one running copy of a backend program. A datacenter runs many tasks of each service.
Requests per second under another name, often written QPS. Google's SRE book warns it's a poor capacity measure when requests cost different amounts.
Jeff Dean's and Google's one-word spelling of data center.
Work waiting to be done, such as messages in a queue that no worker has taken yet.
An AI model trained on large amounts of text that answers by writing text, such as the model behind a chatbot.
Reading one value from RAM. About 100 ns in Jeff Dean's 2009 list.
Reading data in order, one block after the next, which is much faster than jumping around.
A small preview copy of an image.
How much results spread around their average. Dean's 18 ms ignores it, so the real time is longer.
An interface is how you use a piece of software from outside; the implementation is how it works inside.
Amazon Simple Queue Service: a managed queue that holds messages until a worker takes them.
An Amazon SQS metric: the number of messages currently available for retrieval and processing, the queue's backlog.
An Amazon SQS metric: the age of the oldest unprocessed message in the queue, in seconds.
An Application Load Balancer metric in CloudWatch: the number of requests processed. AWS says its most useful statistic is Sum.
How CloudWatch combines a metric's data points over a period, such as Sum, Average or Maximum.
The length of time each CloudWatch data point covers, such as 1 hour or 1 day.

atWork: Pick one queue or service your team sized from a daily number: a worker pool behind an Amazon SQS queue, or an API behind an Application Load Balancer. Read-only access is enough. In CloudWatch, chart the load balancer's RequestCount with the Sum statistic for a busy day, once with a 1-day period and once with a 1-hour period. Divide the busiest hour by the day's total ÷ 24, and that's your real peak factor. For a queue, chart ApproximateNumberOfMessagesVisible and ApproximateAgeOfOldestMessage for the last week. A backlog that grows at the same hour every day and takes hours to drain is a queue sized from the daily average, not the busiest hour: bring it to the next capacity review. Then open the service's design doc and look for the napkin: users, requests a day, the hours they come in, the peak factor, the size of each write, retention, copies and what one server carries. If it isn't there, write it, with each number's source and a date to check it again.

recall.prompt: Your team's notification service sends 8.64 million notifications a day, almost all between 8 and 10 AM. Its design doc says: 8.64 million ÷ 86,400 = 100 a second; a worker sends 50 a second, so 2 workers. Every morning the queue backs up until noon. What went wrong, and how would you redo the sum?

keyIdeas.idea: They arrive in about two hours, not 24, so the real average is 8.64 million ÷ 7,200 = 1,200 a second
Size for the busiest stretch inside those hours, not the average
Workers needed = the rate ÷ 50, plus headroom: 24 busy at that average, about 30 to stay 80% busy, more for the peak
Write the assumptions down and check the new sum against real numbers

recall.model: The sum divided by a whole day, 86,400 seconds, but the notifications go out in about two hours, 7,200 seconds, so the real average is 8.64 million ÷ 7,200 = 1,200 a second, twelve times the doc's 100. Inside those two hours there's a busiest stretch too, so measure it and apply a peak factor. At 50 a second per worker, 1,200 a second keeps 24 workers busy before any peak; with headroom to stay at most 80% busy that's 30, and more for the peak. Fix the doc: write each assumption with its unit, take the peak from the queue's metrics, and check the new number against them next week.

recall.prompt: 100 million requests a day, spread evenly. About how many is that a second?
recall.why: 100,000,000 ÷ 86,400 = 1,157.4. As a check, 100 million is 1 followed by 8 zeros and a day is about 100,000 seconds, so the answer is about 1,000. 69,000 is what dividing by the 1,440 minutes in a day gives: a rate per minute read as a rate per second.

recall.prompt: A backup is 450 GB and the link is 1 Gbps. At best, about how long does the copy take?
recall.why: 450 GB is 450 × 8 = 3,600 gigabits, and 1 Gbps moves 1 gigabit a second, so 3,600 seconds: an hour, at best. 7.5 minutes is 450 seconds, the bytes read as bits.

recall.prompt: A service writes 1 million records a day, 500 bytes each, keeps them 5 years and stores 3 copies. About how much storage is that?
recall.why: 1 million × 500 bytes is 500 MB a day; × 365 is about 183 GB a year; × 5 years is about 910 GB; × 3 copies is about 2.7 TB. 180 GB is one year of one copy, 900 GB forgets the copies, and 22 TB multiplies by 8 as if the bytes were bits.

recall.prompt: In a design review, a teammate says: Don't bother estimating, we'll launch and see what the dashboards say. What do you tell them, in a few sentences?

keyIdeas.idea: An estimate picks the design's shape before you build: one server or many, a cache or not
It's cheap: minutes of arithmetic against weeks of rework or an outage on launch day
Then measure: a load test and the real numbers check the estimate's assumptions

recall.model: Estimating takes minutes and decides things that are expensive to change later: whether one server will do or you need many behind a load balancer, whether the reads need a cache, whether the data fits on one machine. Jeff Dean called it an important skill: estimating a design's performance without having to build it. Launching blind means finding out from an outage. So do the napkin now, write its assumptions in the doc, and then measure: a load test before launch, and the dashboards after, to check every assumption the napkin made.

coldCase.update: UPDATE, a year later. Coldharbour Cars has an app now. In November it took 72,000 bookings, so Mr Vasko's nephew sized the booking server on a napkin of his own: 72,000 ÷ 30 days = 2,400 a day, ÷ 86,400 = 0.03 a second, and one small server does 150 a second. On New Year's Eve the app took 4,500 bookings in the hour after one, and every waiting rider's map asks where their cab is every 5 seconds, for about 10 minutes. At 1:20 every map froze, every cab stood still on every screen, and one cab none of us had sent sat outside the office with its light on.
coldCase.prompt: Reply to OP. What did the nephew's napkin miss, and how should he redo it?

keyIdeas.idea: Every booking brings about 120 map refreshes, so reads swamp writes
Size for the busiest hour of the busiest night, not November's daily average
4,500 × 120 ÷ 3,600 = 150 reads a second, the whole small server, so add headroom: at least 2
Cut the reads: cache the cab positions or refresh less often

coldCase.model: The napkin sized the bookings, the writes, and only their November daily average. But every booking brings reads: a map asking every 5 seconds for about 10 minutes is about 120 asks per booking, so reads outnumber writes 120 to 1. And New Year's Eve's hour after one is the peak: 4,500 bookings is 1.25 a second, and 4,500 × 120 = 540,000 map asks in the hour, 150 a second, exactly the small server's 150 with nothing to spare, so every map froze. Redo it from the busiest hour with the reads counted: 150 reads a second plus 1.25 writes, then headroom, at least 2 small servers, and cut the reads: cache the cab positions for a few seconds, or refresh every 15 seconds instead of 5, which divides the reads by 3.
